prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms to inter-laboratory agreement at a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part prize for the optical lattice clock, Katori and Ye, and my position is firmer than in round 1 because the chair's summary shows what the convergence rests on. Six of eight configurations name the same pair, and no member proposes a different one. Nobody has produced a scientific objection that survives: every supporter records the same lineage reservation, and none shows it defeats the case. In one sentence, what is new relative to 2005 and 2012: the 2005 prize gave the optical frequency ruler and the 2012 prize gave control of single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different measurement architecture, in which light shifts of the two clock levels cancel at the magic wavelength, so that thousands of neutral atoms are held free of Doppler and recoil shifts and interrogated in parallel. That is what turns accuracy at 10^-18 into stability reachable in practical averaging times. As an instrument builder I weigh three things: a new regime reached by a new technique, independent reproduction, and use beyond the inventors. JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree at that level in direct comparisons, and the instrument already resolves gravitational redshift over millimetres and constrains constants and dark matter. I treat the unfinished redefinition of the second as timing, not evidence. The citation should say lattice scheme and 10^-18 and should not mention the redefinition. I do not think a second part is workable or needed: B015 plus any three-name entry exceeds the limit, and the only pairing on the table, B040 with Halzen alone, fails on credit.
statement.case_against: The lineage objection remains the strongest. A critic can say that 2005 and 2012 already honoured the enabling tools and that a gain from 10^-15 to 10^-18 is a large quantitative step, not a new principle. I answer it with the architecture argument above, but I accept that this is a judgement about degree against kind, and that Johansson is right that B015 is weaker if the committee wants a new phenomenon in the statutory sense. A prize for a measurement technique is still an invention in the sense of the statutes, but I would not claim it is uncontested. Attribution is the second risk: Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups also contributed, and two names cannot represent the field. Third, atomic physics is outside my own expertise, so on the clock detail I am relying on Lindroth and Kroll and, if the committee agrees, an external reviewer. The redefinition of the second is still prospective, and waiting a year would cost little scientifically, though I see no reason in the physics why the result will be less secure then.

responses.point: Kroll supports B015 with a citation running from the magic-wavelength concept to the 10^-18 level, and the chair asked him and Lindroth to draft wording that separates it from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. He also discloses time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, near Ye's group.
responses.response: I accept your wording as the base, since it names both the scheme and the regime. I have added that the clock opens a new regime of precision measurement, so that the citation says what was gained and not only a number. I would keep the redefinition of the second out of it. On your Boulder year, I think the committee should record it, as you ask, but I do not see it as disqualifying: you have no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and your preference matches those of members with no such tie, Lindroth, Mehlig and Johansson. I would still ask you to be the one who confirms that the technical statement of the magic-wavelength condition in the citation is accurate, since you are closer to the field than I am.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether a metrology achievement counts as a discovery and whether the demonstrated 10^-18 performance suffices without awaiting the SI redefinition. She also says that if a second part is wanted, Zoller and Cirac recurring in B011 and B016 would constrain the choice.
responses.response: On the first point, my answer is that the statutes speak of discovery or invention, and the lattice clock is an invention with demonstrated physics consequences, which is how I would read it. On waiting, I would not wait: the evidence is the clock-to-clock agreement we have now, and a prize that rests on a future redefinition would be resting on the wrong thing. Your point on the second part is persuasive and is a further reason I now prefer a single part. Any second entry with three names breaks the three-person limit, and B011 and B016 share Cirac and Zoller, so neither fits well beside Katori and Ye. If you or Kroll can say which other clock groups an expert would consider decisive, I would want that said in the committee record even if the credited pair stays.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B051 with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, concedes that omitting Mele is the weak point, and says he would support B015 if the attribution of B051 cannot be resolved. He also holds that the clock case is a gain in precision, not a new principle.
responses.response: I have thought about your trio again. It is a trio I would also pick from the supplied names, and I accept the experimental case as robust, but it is outside my competence to settle whether Mele can be separated from Kane. If the committee cannot answer that, as you say, I think the Kane-Mele pair is intact and one of Molenkamp or Hasan has to drop out, which makes the credit contested in a way that B015's is not. I do not think this disqualifies the field: it could be a strong candidate in a later year once an expert report settles the credit. On precision versus principle, we remain apart, but your own alternative list includes B015 and you say you would support it, so I hope the final ballot can reflect that shared fallback.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B017 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) as a door-opener, accepts that the superconducting mechanism and credit for Cao and others are open, and says she would not oppose B015. She asked whether the clock is a discovery or invention in the statutory sense.
responses.response: I take the door-opener argument seriously, and the reproduction across many groups is real. My concern, which you share, is that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and twist-angle disorder complicates reproducibility. For a prize I want the physical understanding to be stable, and that is where the clock is ahead: every systematic is accounted for in clock-to-clock comparisons. The credit for B017 is also not clean, with Cao outside your three names, and I would rather see that settled by time than guessed at. I agree that B017 is a serious candidate for a later year, and I have put it on my alternatives list for that reason. On your statutory question, I regard the lattice clock as an invention that has already produced measurements nobody could make before, and I hope that lets you treat B015 as acceptable.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers a two-part prize pairing B015 with B040 (Katori, Ye and Halzen) and argues that Halzen's conception of the cubic-kilometre detector is unusually identifiable, but concedes that single-name credit is the weak point.
responses.response: You asked whether I would drop B040 as a preferred part, and I do, for a prize this year. I argued Halzen's role at opening and I still believe the conception of the cubic-kilometre detector was decisive. But I do not know how to name the AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES pioneers and the IceCube builders in a way I could defend, and the three-person limit forbids adding them to B015. The diffuse flux is firm, whereas the source identifications are still at moderate significance, so waiting costs little and a later citation to neutrino astronomy could be more robust. I declare my own field interest in this below. I would keep B040 on my alternatives list, and I would welcome an expert historical report on who established the diffuse flux, but I cannot support a two-part prize on today's credit.

uncertainties: Whether the architecture argument, many atoms at the magic wavelength with first-order shifts removed, is accepted by the committee as a new regime and not as an increment on the 2005 and 2012 prizes. This is a judgement I cannot settle from my own field.

Whether Katori and Ye alone are adequate credit given Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and whether an external reviewer would name someone decisive. No member has proposed a different pair.
Whether the committee should wait a year for the redefinition of the second, which I regard as timing and not evidence.
Whether a defensible three-name credit for IceCube exists at all, and whether a single-name credit for Halzen would stand up to expert review.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Katori, Ye or the clock community is apparent from my profile, and I have no collaboration with the groups at JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST or SYRTE. My research is in cosmic-ray, gamma-ray and X-ray astroparticle instrumentation, and I work in the Fermi-LAT collaboration, so I have a field-level interest in B040 (IceCube) and B013 (gamma-ray burst afterglows), with no recorded personal or institutional tie to any credited name. Neither is in my preferred configuration. If either enters the final configuration I would declare this interest and defer to colleagues on that part. I disclose that B015 is outside my expertise and I rely on Lindroth and Kroll.
